newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA'S INSIDER TRADING REPORT COMES UNDER FIRE.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA'S INSIDER TRADING REPORT COMES UNDER FIRE.

text.p: A dissenting member of a government-appointed task group on insider trading in South Africa has criticised the team's recommendations as potentially harmful to the country's securities markets.
Koos Stassen, chief legal adviser to life assurance giant Old Mutual, issued a minority report rejecting the task group's proposals.
"The recommendations contained in the report...will criminalise normal and honest conduct by participants in the securities markets, including the man in the street," Stassen said in his report.
He criticised the proposals as being unduly wide in scope, going further than any insider trading prohibitions worldwide, without justification.
The recommendations would make it impossible for employees and directors to trade shares in their own firms without breaking the law, he said.

The task group, chaired by Mervyn King, recommended a separate law on insider trading and its classification as a civil and criminal transgression. The team also made proposals on compensation and plea bargains in prosecutions.
South Africa is burdened with the reputation of a hot-bed of insider trading, with well-reported incidents of trading in company shares ahead of major announcements.
The cases are notoriously difficult to prove and there has never been a successful prosecution in South Africa.
Bond traders have also complained about irregular leaks of key economic data released by government departments and official agencies.

"Several of the measures proposed will also be unconstitutional, such as the imposition of presumptions of guilt, the granting to the FSB (Financial Services Board) of the power to bind the courts to the result of plea-bargaining and the proposed investigatory powers," he said.

Stassen said the group had been scheduled to meet to discuss several members' concerns about the scope of the proposals, but the meeting was cancelled and the report was issued in May without the discussion taking place.

He also recommended that disclosure requirements of the various securities markets be improved to promote better access to information "and remove a large part of the most important cause of insider trading".
Stassen said several groups with interests in the securities markets agreed with his report and would be supporting it in representations to Finance Minister Trevor Manuel.

The King document is open for public comment until June 30, after which a final report will be presented to the Policy Board for Financial Services and Regulations, which in turn will make recommendations to Manuel.
